section.title: Judgment for Idolatry in Egypt
section.sectionRationale: Settled in Egypt against God's word, the remnant does not merely fail to repent, it doubles down on the very sin that destroyed Jerusalem, openly burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and blaming their troubles on having ever stopped. Jeremiah's final recorded confrontation with them ends in a flat impasse: they refuse to listen, and God gives Pharaoh Hophra's own downfall as the sign proving whose word will stand, His or theirs.
section.thesis: A people relocated by their own disobedience still refuse to change, defending their idolatry to Jeremiah's face and blaming disaster on the very repentance that never truly happened, so God gives them one final sign to prove that His word, not their comforting nostalgia, will stand.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: judgment recalled, Jerusalem's ruin traced directly to idolatry; the people's brazen refusal, defending the Queen of Heaven to Jeremiah's face; Jeremiah's reply naming exactly why the disaster came; and a sign given, Pharaoh Hophra's coming downfall, to prove whose word stands.

units.label: Judgment recalled: Jerusalem's ruin from idolatry
units.note: the lesson of the ruins, unlearned

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews living in the land of Egypt, in Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Memphis, and in the land of Pathros:

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: You have seen all the disaster that I brought against Jerusalem and all the cities of Judah; and behold, they lie today in ruins and desolation

because of the evil they have done. 
They provoked Me to anger by continuing to burn incense and to serve other gods that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew.
Yet I sent you all My servants the prophets again and again, saying: ‘Do not do this detestable thing that I hate.’
But they did not listen or incline their ears; they did not turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods.
Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, so that they have become the desolate ruin they are today.

So now, this is what the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves by cutting off from Judah man and woman, child and infant, leaving yourselves without a remnant?

Why are you provoking Me to anger by the work of your hands by burning incense to other gods in the land of Egypt, where you have gone to reside? 
As a result, you will be cut off and will become an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth.

Have you forgotten the wickedness of your fathers and of the kings of Judah and their wives, as well as the wickedness that you and your wives committed in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence, nor have they followed My instruction or the statutes that I set before you and your fathers.
Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I will set My face to bring disaster and to cut off all Judah.

And I will take away the remnant of Judah who have resolved to go to the land of Egypt to reside there; they will meet their end. They will all fall by the sword or be consumed by famine. From the least to the greatest, they will die by sword or famine; and they will become an object of cursing and horror, of vilification and reproach.
I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem, by sword and famine and plague,

so that none of the remnant of Judah who have gone to reside in Egypt will escape or survive to return to the land of Judah, where they long to return and live; for none will return except a few fugitives.”

units.label: The people refuse, defend the Queen of Heaven
units.note: blaming disaster on the wrong cause

verses.text: Then all the men who knew that their wives were burning incense to other gods, and all the women standing by, a great assembly, along with all the people living in the land of Egypt and in Pathros, said to Jeremiah,
“As for the word you have spoken to us in the name of the LORD, we will not listen to you!

Instead, we will do everything we vowed to do: We will burn incense to the {{malkath|Queen of Heaven}} and offer drink offerings to her, just as we, our fathers, our kings, and our officials did in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem. 
At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster.
But from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine.”

“Moreover,” said the women, “when we burned incense to the Queen of Heaven and poured out drink offerings to her, was it without our husbands' knowledge that we made sacrificial cakes in her image and poured out drink offerings to her?”

units.label: Jeremiah's reply: this is why the disaster came

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, both men and women, who were answering him,

“As for the incense you burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, you, your fathers, your kings, your officials, and the people of the land, did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?
So the LORD could no longer endure the evil deeds and detestable acts you committed, and your land became a desolation, a horror, and an object of cursing, without inhabitant, as it is this day.

Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD, and did not {{shama|obey}} the voice of the LORD or walk in His instruction, His statutes, and His testimonies, this disaster has befallen you, as you see today.”

units.label: A sign given: Pharaoh Hophra's downfall

verses.text: Then Jeremiah said to all the people, including all the women, “Hear the word of the LORD, all those of Judah who are in the land of Egypt.

This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: As for you and your wives, you have spoken with your mouths and fulfilled with your hands your words: ‘We will surely perform our vows that we have made to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and to pour out drink offerings to her.’ Go ahead, then, do what you have promised! Keep your vows!

Nevertheless, hear the word of the LORD, all you people of Judah living in Egypt: Behold, I have sworn by My great name, says the LORD, that never again will any man of Judah living in the land of Egypt invoke My name or say, ‘As surely as the Lord GOD lives.’
I am watching over them for harm and not for good, and every man of Judah who is in the land of Egypt will meet his end by sword or famine, until they are finished off.
Those who escape the sword will return from Egypt to Judah, few in number, and the whole remnant of Judah who went to dwell in the land of Egypt will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!
This will be a sign to you that I will punish you in this place, declares the LORD, so that you may know that My threats of harm against you will surely stand.

This is what the LORD says: Behold, I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of his enemies who seek his life, just as I delivered Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the enemy who was seeking his life.”

malkath.gloss: The Queen of Heaven, likely a title for the goddess Ishtar or Astarte, worshiped with incense, drink offerings, and sacrificial cakes shaped in her image. The people credit her, not the LORD, for their past prosperity, inverting cause and effect entirely.

shama.gloss: To hear, and by extension to obey, since in Hebrew thought truly hearing a command means doing it. Jeremiah names the people's failure to shama, obey, the voice of the LORD as the actual, plain cause of the disaster they insist on blaming elsewhere.

basic.context: In Egypt, the very place God had warned them not to flee to, the remnant does not repent but doubles down, openly burning incense and pouring drink offerings to the Queen of Heaven, a pagan goddess. When Jeremiah confronts them, they answer with a stunning inversion of cause and effect: they credit their old idolatry with the prosperity they remember and blame their recent troubles on having stopped it, not on the sin itself. Jeremiah restates plainly that their idolatry, not its interruption, destroyed Jerusalem, and God gives a specific, falsifiable sign, the coming downfall of Pharaoh Hophra, to prove once for all whose word will actually stand.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the starkest picture in the book of a hardened conscience rationalizing sin by rewriting its own history, remembering false prosperity under idolatry and blaming disaster on repentance rather than rebellion. Read straightforwardly, the passage does not merely describe stubbornness, it shows a whole community organizing its collective memory around a self-serving lie, and Jeremiah's plain restatement of the facts, verses 21 to 23, is offered as the corrective standard for testing any such comfortable rewriting of history.
basic.originalLanguages: The people insist on continuing worship of the malkath hashamayim, the Queen of Heaven, crediting her rather than the LORD for their prosperity. Jeremiah's answer turns on shama, to hear and obey, the one thing they conspicuously did not do, and their disaster follows directly from that failure, not from any change in ritual practice toward a pagan goddess.
basic.typology: The people's readiness to keep worshiping a false queen of heaven, imagined as the true source of provision, anticipates every later idolatry that credits creation or human power for gifts that belong to the Creator alone.
basic.christ: This chapter shows humanity's native tendency at its bluntest, worshiping the creature rather than the Creator and calling that worship the source of blessing, exactly what Paul describes in Romans 1:25. Christ, the true and better provider of every good gift, exposes and reverses this exchange, calling people not to a queen of heaven but to the living God who alone gives daily bread, and whose Son alone secures the true and lasting rest that idols only ever promised falsely.
basic.god: God's patience has clearly reached its limit with this generation; having sent prophet after prophet and endured Jerusalem's fall itself as an object lesson, He now simply states what will happen and lets a falsifiable sign, Pharaoh Hophra's downfall, prove His word true. Yet even in pronouncing near total judgment, God specifies that a few fugitives will return, verse 14, and that some will survive, verse 28, keeping His promise of an unbroken remnant even here.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 1:25 describes exchanging the truth of God for a lie and worshiping the creature rather than the Creator. Deuteronomy 4:19 forbids worship of the host of heaven, the very category the Queen of Heaven belongs to. Jeremiah 7:18 already described this same worship, families baking cakes for the queen of heaven, back in Judah before the exile. 1 Kings 22:28 records a similar falsifiable prophetic test, if you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me.
basic.oneStory: A remnant that fled to Egypt for safety instead doubles down on the idolatry that destroyed their homeland, rewriting their own history to blame repentance rather than rebellion, until God gives a plain, testable sign to settle whose word will stand. This is the whole Bible's diagnosis of the human heart, quick to worship the creature and call it blessing, a diagnosis answered only when Christ turns hearts back to worship the Creator alone.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 44 is the only extended debate in the book. The pattern is accusation, answer, counter answer, verdict. Verses 1 to 14 are God's case, 15 to 19 the people's reply, 20 to 23 Jeremiah's rebuttal, and 24 to 30 the sentence with its sign. Elsewhere the people are mostly silent or deflect; here they speak at length and with confidence, and the author lets them state their theology in full.

The opening address is carefully layered. God first recalls Jerusalem's ruin, 44:2 to 6, then turns to the Egyptian community with a 'Why?' in 44:7 and 44:8, and only then pronounces the sentence in 44:11 to 14. The shape moves from the past, to the present question, to the future. The repeated phrase 'to this day,' 44:2, 6, 10, 22 and 23, ties the ruin of Judah to the people's continued behaviour. The ruins are offered as evidence in the case.

The reply of the people is built on a claim about cause and effect: we burned incense and had bread and saw no harm, we stopped and have lacked everything, 44:17 and 44:18. The women's rejoinder in verse 19 closes off a possible escape for the husbands by insisting that the husbands knew. Jeremiah's answer in 21 to 23 matches the form, but with a different set of facts: God remembered the incense, and the disaster came because of it.

The sentence closes the chapter with a sarcastic permission, 'Go ahead, then, do what you have promised,' 44:25, and then a sign in 44:30 that sets Hophra's fall alongside Zedekiah's. The final verse is the only place in the chapter where the focus shifts to a named foreign king, and it echoes the sign at Tahpanhes in chapter 43. Egypt is not a refuge but a mirror of Judah's own king.
context.historical:
The Jews of 44:1 are settled in four regions: Migdol and Tahpanhes in the north eastern delta, Memphis to the south, and Pathros, the name for Upper Egypt. The BSB footnotes note that the Hebrew has Noph where the Septuagint has Memphis. The refugees of chapter 43 had spread across the length of the country. Later evidence confirms that Jewish communities lived in Egypt for generations. The Aramaic papyri from Elephantine, a Jewish military colony in the far south, come from the fifth century BC and show a community with its own temple, though that is a later period than Jeremiah's.

The Queen of Heaven was a deity worshiped with incense, drink offerings and cakes baked in her image, Jeremiah 7:18 and 44:19. Her identity is not certain. Interpreters have proposed the Mesopotamian Ishtar, the Canaanite Astarte, or an Egyptian figure such as Isis, and it is quite possible that in popular religion these roles overlapped. What the text shows is a household cult in which women had a leading part, and the women's own comment in 44:19 shows they saw themselves as acting within family religion, with husbands' approval.

The people's memory of prosperity probably points back to the long years when Judah's religion was open to other gods. Manasseh reigned fifty-five years, 2 Kings 21:1 to 3, and rebuilt the high places. Josiah then removed the objects made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven, 2 Kings 23:4 to 5, but he died at Megiddo, 2 Kings 23:29, and the nation's fortunes declined sharply afterward. Some readers think the refugees tied that decline to the reform. This is a plausible reading, though the text does not name Josiah.

Pharaoh Hophra, whom Greek writers call Apries, reigned from about 589 BC and lost power to his general Amasis about 570. The fulfilment of 44:30 is usually placed in that coup. The oracle therefore fits the period when the refugees were still in Egypt and could check the claim against events.
context.canonical:
The chapter gathers up a long line of prophetic argument about idolatry. Jeremiah 7:16 to 20 had already described the families gathering wood and kneading dough for the Queen of Heaven, and had told Jeremiah not to intercede. The earlier chapter described the scene in Judah, and this chapter shows the practice continuing, unrepentant, in Egypt. The people's defence also finds an earlier answer in Hosea 2:5 to 8, where Israel says that her lovers give her bread, water, wool and oil, and the Lord responds that He was the one who gave. The idolater credits the wrong giver.

The test of a prophet that the chapter builds into its ending comes from Deuteronomy 18:21 to 22: a word spoken in the Lord's name that does not come true is not from Him. Jeremiah offers a falsifiable sign. First Kings 22:28 shows the same logic, Micaiah staking his message on the king's return. The Law's ban on worshiping the host of heaven, Deuteronomy 4:19, stands under the whole dispute.

Other prophets echo the scene. Ezekiel 8:14 sees women weeping for Tammuz at the temple gate, another case of women leading a rival cult, and Ezekiel 20:39 offers a similar sarcastic permission, 'Go and serve your idols,' before promising that they will afterward listen. Ezekiel 29 and 30 foretell Egypt's own desolation, and Ezekiel 30:18 names Tahpanhes, which gives a second witness to Jeremiah's claim that the refuge will fail.

In the New Testament Paul's statement in Romans 1:21 to 25 reads like a summary of this chapter in theological terms: people who knew God did not honour Him, and exchanged the truth for a lie. Paul's words at Lystra, Acts 14:17, supply the answer to the people's claim about provision. God has never left Himself without a witness, giving rain, fruitful seasons and food. First Corinthians 10:20 to 22 then gives the pastoral counterpart, that believers cannot share the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wanted exiles and later readers to see that the destruction of Jerusalem was not a mystery. The people in Egypt looked at the same facts as God and drew the opposite conclusion. The chapter is a case study in interpretation: the same ruins can be read as proof that the old worship had been abandoned or as proof that it had been persisted in. Jeremiah's point in 44:21 to 23 is that the Lord kept an account, and that the record settles the dispute.

He also wanted to show how a community protects itself from correction. The leaders do not argue about particular evidence. They appeal to experience, to tradition, to the shared practice of kings and officials, and to the family. Nothing in the reply engages what Jeremiah said about the prophets who had been sent again and again. A word that would require a change of life is dismissed as a message from an unwelcome source, 44:16.

At the same time the chapter closes with two notes that matter for any hearer who still has an ear. The Lord promises a sign, 44:29, so that the matter will be settled by events. And the Lord promises that a few will return, 44:14 and 44:28. The author was not recording a closed door. He was telling readers in exile that the remnant would be small, that survival would be by mercy and that the way back to the land would be a narrow one.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a worship practice and the arguments used to defend it. It does not offer the arguments as reasoning to be adopted. The people's inference, that prosperity proves a practice is right and hardship proves it wrong, is recorded in order to be refuted. It is not a general rule of cause and effect, and Scripture elsewhere shows that the righteous may suffer and the wicked may prosper, as in Job and Psalm 73.

The command that does carry over is the ban on worshiping any rival to the Lord, Exodus 20:3 to 5, and the call to attribute every good gift to its true giver. First John 5:21 closes with the instruction to keep from idols, and the idols of any age are usually the same, whatever supplies security, success or provision. Believers are also meant to notice the pattern of rewriting history. When a community prefers the past it remembers over the past that happened, it cannot repent.

It would be wrong to apply the sentence of judgment on the Egyptian community directly to any group today, or to treat every disaster as the verdict of a particular sin. Jeremiah knew the cause of this disaster because the Lord had told him and had sent prophets for generations. What we may say is that God's patience has an end, and that the call to turn is always given before the sentence.

debates.question: Who is the Queen of Heaven?

views.label: A Mesopotamian goddess such as Ishtar
views.case: Ishtar was called queen of heaven in Mesopotamian texts, and cult cakes in a goddess's image fit that world. Judah had been under Assyrian influence in the seventh century, and Manasseh's reign opened the land to foreign worship, 2 Kings 21:3.

views.label: A Canaanite or Egyptian figure such as Astarte or Isis
views.case: The cult is practised in Egypt and was inherited from Judah, so a Canaanite goddess adopted into local religion is plausible. Some suggest a blending of Astarte with Egyptian devotion once the refugees settled.

debates.bearing: The text never settles the name, and Jeremiah's argument does not depend on it. Whatever she was called, she was a created rival to the Lord, covered by the ban on worshiping the host of heaven, Deuteronomy 4:19.

debates.question: What historical event do the people have in mind when they say the troubles began when they stopped?

views.label: The reform of Josiah
views.case: Josiah removed the objects of foreign worship, 2 Kings 23:4 to 5, and soon afterward died in battle, 2 Kings 23:29. Judah's slide began from there, so a popular reading would link the reform and the trouble.

views.label: A more general memory of earlier years
views.case: The people speak of kings and officials who also burned incense, 44:17, and Manasseh's long reign was a time of relative stability under an open religion. Their memory could be a loose collective story, not tied to a single date.

debates.bearing: The text leaves it open. In both readings the people confuse a sequence of events with a cause. Jeremiah answers with the prophets' warnings across generations, 44:4, which show that the sin came before the disaster and not the other way round.

study.originalLanguages:
The wording of the chapter shows how carefully the argument is built. First, the idiom behind 'again and again' in 44:4. The footnote gives the literal form, 'the prophets, rising up early and sending them.' It is a phrase characteristic of Jeremiah, as in Jeremiah 7:25 and 25:4, and the image is of a householder up before dawn to send messengers. The Lord is portrayed as someone who started early and kept sending. The refusal in 44:5 is a refusal of a patient and insistent God.

Second, 'detestable thing' in 44:4 and 44:22 is the Hebrew word for what is an abomination to the Lord, the standard label for idolatrous practice in Deuteronomy. In 44:4 the word is joined with a verb of hating, 'this detestable thing that I hate,' so the Lord uses the strongest language of His own revulsion.

Third, a play on the word for 'disaster' or 'evil.' The same Hebrew word, ra'ah, stands for the harm that fell and for the wickedness that caused it. In 44:17 the people say, 'we saw no disaster,' and in 44:3 and 44:22 God speaks of the evil they did. The verbal match makes the point that they will not see the connection: the harm they suffered was the answer to the harm they did.

Fourth, the verb 'stand' in 44:25 and 44:28. In 44:25 the Lord says in an ironic tone that they are going to 'confirm' their vows, a form that doubles the verb, and the same root appears in 44:28 and 44:29: 'will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs.' The vow they were so careful to establish will be tested against the word of the Lord that stands.

Fifth, the idiom of the mouth. In 44:17 the Hebrew speaks of what 'went out from our mouth,' and in 44:25 God says they have spoken with their mouths and fulfilled with their hands. In 44:26 the Lord says His name will not be called 'in the mouth' of any man of Judah in Egypt. Those who put the vow to the Queen of Heaven in their mouths lose the right to put the Lord's name there. Finally, 'set My face' in 44:11 is the same idiom used in 42:15 for the people's own resolve, so the Lord's resolve now meets theirs.

typology.type: The false provider who takes the credit for daily bread, Jeremiah 44:17 to 18
typology.fulfillment: The people think the Queen of Heaven supplied bread and good things. Hosea 2:8 states the same mistake, that Israel did not know it was the Lord who gave the grain. The true provider is revealed in Christ, who says 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35, and teaches His followers to pray 'Give us this day our daily bread,' Matthew 6:11. The correspondence is that every age has a false giver. The escalation is that the Giver comes in person and gives Himself. The type falls short because the false queen never gave anything, while Christ gives life.

typology.type: The cup and table of a rival cult, Jeremiah 44:17 to 19
typology.fulfillment: The drink offerings and the cakes in the queen's image are a rival meal. Paul sets the same contrast in the church: 'You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too,' 1 Corinthians 10:21. The meal of the Lord's table is the redeemed replacement for the household cult of idolatry. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's day offered no table of the true God in Egypt, while the church's table is open and effective by the blood of Christ.

typology.type: The few fugitives who escape and return, Jeremiah 44:14 and 44:28
typology.fulfillment: The promise that a small number would escape the sword and come back is the thread of the remnant. Paul quotes Isaiah, 'only the remnant will be saved,' Romans 9:27, and speaks of 'a remnant chosen by grace,' Romans 11:5. The correspondence is that the survivors are saved by mercy and not by numbers or merit. The type is imperfect: Jeremiah's fugitives come back to a ruined land, while the remnant in Christ is brought into a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most directly by exposing the need He answers. The people credit a false queen for bread and good things, and the effect is a community that cannot repent because it believes the cause of its trouble is the cure. Paul describes the same heart in Romans 1:25, and Jesus names it when He says the light came into the world and people loved the darkness, John 3:19. The final hardness of this community, 'we will not listen to you,' 44:16, is the same refusal Jesus meets in His parable of the nobleman, whose subjects say, 'We do not want this man to rule over us,' Luke 19:14.

It leads to Christ as the true provider. The people's argument was about who supplies food and security. Jesus claims that role in terms the chapter's idolatry cannot match: 'I am the bread of life,' John 6:35. He teaches His followers to ask the Father for daily bread, Matthew 6:11, and Paul tells pagans at Lystra that the God who made heaven and earth is the one who fills their hearts with food and gladness, Acts 14:17. What the Queen of Heaven was believed to give, Christ gives, and gives truly.

It leads to Christ as the one whose word stands. The contest in 44:28 is 'whose word will stand, Mine or theirs.' Jesus claims the same permanence when He says, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away,' Luke 21:33. Hophra's fall will test Jeremiah's word within a generation. The resurrection is the sign that Jesus' word stands beyond every generation. In John 8:31 to 32 He tells those who believed Him that continuing in His word is the mark of a true disciple, in contrast to the people who walked away from the word of the Lord in Egypt.

It leads to Christ in the call to a table. Paul draws the line that the household cult of Jeremiah 44 could not draw: you cannot share the Lord's cup and the cup of demons, 1 Corinthians 10:21. The Lord's Supper is where the true God gives Himself and demands exclusive loyalty.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage is not secretly about Christ in every detail. The Queen of Heaven is not a code name, and Pharaoh Hophra is not a figure of Satan. The chapter points to Christ by its diagnosis of idolatry, its contest between two words, and its small remnant, and by the New Testament's own use of these themes.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all a God who explains Himself. He does not simply destroy. In 44:2 to 6 He lays out the case, recalls the ruins as evidence, reminds the people that He sent His servants the prophets again and again, and asks real questions: 'Why are you doing such great harm to yourselves?' 44:7. The question treats the harm as self inflicted, which is a form of love, since He is naming the people's own interest. He argues with them because He wants them to answer.

He is jealous in the biblical sense. The language of provocation in 44:3 and 44:8 reflects the claim of Exodus 20:5 that He is a jealous God, who will not share His glory with a rival. It is not petty. The idol takes credit for the gifts and leaves the giver forgotten, and God cares about being known as the giver, which is the basis for gratitude and trust. A God who allowed rivals to take His name would be a God who did not care for His people.

He is patient to a fault. The prophets rose early and were sent again and again, and 2 Chronicles 36:15 says that He did so because He had compassion. He does not act until every appeal has been spent. This makes the judgment of 44:11 to 14 the settled response of a God who first spoke in many ways.

He is true. He holds history in His hand and uses it as a witness. The sign of Hophra, 44:30, is offered precisely because He is willing to be tested by events. A God who stakes His word on what will happen in a pharaoh's palace is confident that His word will stand, 44:28.

He is sovereign over the nations. Pharaoh, whose power the refugees counted on, will be given into the hands of his enemies, just as Zedekiah was given to Nebuchadnezzar. The same hand governs Judah's king and Egypt's king, and the one who sets one down sets the other down.

He is merciful even in judgment. 'None will return except a few fugitives,' 44:14, and 'those who escape the sword will return,' 44:28, show that He keeps a remnant even here. The sentence is severe, but it never leaves the covenant promise unfulfilled.

For worship, the chapter asks us to take the giver more seriously than the gift. Gratitude is the form that trust takes, and it belongs to the Lord alone. It also warns that tolerance of rivals is not neutral, because the Lord answers every act of worship by who is receiving it.

crossReferences.note: The earlier description of the cult in Judah, with children gathering wood, fathers lighting the fire and women kneading dough for the Queen of Heaven. The chapter in Egypt shows the same family liturgy carried into exile. Jeremiah is also told not to intercede, which explains the severity of the later sentence.

Israel claims that her lovers give her bread, water, wool, linen, oil and drink, and the Lord replies that He is the real giver. The accusation of Jeremiah 44:17 is the same lie in the mouths of a later generation: giving credit to an idol for what the Lord provided.

The test of a prophet is whether the word comes true. Jeremiah's sign in 44:29 to 30 applies it directly, since Hophra's fall would show whose word stood. The people are given a way to know and still choose not to hear.

The Law forbids bowing to the sun, moon, stars and all the host of heaven. A queen of heaven belongs to this category, so the worship in Jeremiah 44 breaks a clear command that Israel had been given before entering the land.

The Lord speaks with similar irony, 'Go and serve your idols,' then promises that afterward Israel will listen. It reads in the same key as Jeremiah 44:25, where the permission to keep the vows is a judgment that lets the refusal run its course.

Josiah's reform removed the articles made for Baal, Asherah and the host of heaven. The refugees' claim that trouble began when they stopped may reflect memory of this reform, though the text does not say so. It shows that the removal of idols had been commanded and carried out by a king.

Paul's account of how people exchange the truth of God for a lie reads as a doctrinal summary of Jeremiah 44. People who know the Lord withhold gratitude, drift into foolish thinking, and worship the creature. The refugees give the story a face.

Paul tells the crowd at Lystra that God has not left Himself without testimony, giving rain, fruitful seasons and food. It is the New Testament reply to the claim in Jeremiah 44:17 that an idol provides plenty. Provision is a witness to the true God.

Paul says that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons and that believers cannot share the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. It carries the logic of Jeremiah's rebuke into the church and asks for undivided loyalty at the Lord's table.

Ezekiel promises that idols in Memphis will be destroyed and that the day will be darkened in Tahpanhes. It is a second prophetic witness that Egypt is no safe harbour, and the places named are the same towns where the refugees of Jeremiah 44:1 settled.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the human problem is not only that people disobey but that they interpret. The serpent offered a story in which God was holding something back, and Eve took it. Israel in the wilderness remembered Egypt's food and forgot its bondage, Numbers 11:5. In Jeremiah 44 the refugees do the same thing on a national scale: they rewrite the past so that idolatry looks like the source of plenty, and the Lord looks like the cause of lack. It is the old lie in new clothes, a lie about who gives.

What the chapter sets up is the question of how such a people can ever be changed. Argument does not do it, since Jeremiah gives the plainest reply possible and they answer, 'we will not listen.' Judgment does not do it by itself, since Jerusalem's ruins were in plain sight. The prophets are left saying that something more than correction is required. Jeremiah 31:33 promises a law written on the heart, and Ezekiel 36:26 a new heart. The chapter shows why the promise was needed.

The remnant is the thread that holds the hope. A few fugitives return, 44:28, as a few had always been preserved, and the line runs through the exile to the return and finally to the remnant chosen by grace, Romans 11:5. Christ is the true Israel in whom the remnant is gathered. He feeds the people the false queen could not feed, bears the judgment the idolater deserves, and puts the Spirit in those who believe so that they can hear.

The end of the story answers the false claim of provision. In the new creation there is no temple, no queen and no rival, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The tree of life bears fruit every month, Revelation 22:2, and the people who were once tempted to thank anything but the Giver will give Him thanks without end. Gratitude that was misdirected in Egypt is finally put in the right place.

quiz.q: What does God say destroyed Jerusalem and the cities of Judah?

options.text: Their persistent idolatry, burning incense and serving other gods despite repeated warnings from the prophets.
options.note: Verses 2 to 6 state this cause directly and repeatedly.

options.text: A famine unrelated to any spiritual cause.
options.note: The disaster is explicitly tied to idolatry and disobedience, not an unrelated natural famine.

options.text: Their failure to pay tribute to Babylon on time.
options.note: No mention is made of tribute payments as the cause; the stated cause is persistent idolatry.

options.text: The moral failure of a single king alone.
options.note: The text spreads responsibility broadly, kings, officials, and people alike, not one king in isolation.

quiz.q: How do the people in Egypt respond to Jeremiah's warning against continuing to worship the Queen of Heaven?

options.text: They flatly refuse to listen and insist on continuing their vows to her, crediting her with their past prosperity.
options.note: Verses 16 to 18 record this direct refusal and their claimed reasoning.

options.text: They immediately repent and destroy their idols.
options.note: They do the opposite, openly refusing to stop and insisting on continuing the worship.

options.text: They ask Jeremiah to pray for forgiveness on their behalf.
options.note: They explicitly refuse to listen to Jeremiah's word at all, rather than asking for intercession.

options.text: Only the men continue the practice while the women object.
options.note: Both the men and the women defend the practice together, as verse 19's women's testimony shows.

quiz.q: What reasoning do the people give for continuing to worship the Queen of Heaven?

options.text: They claim they had plenty of food and no disaster while worshiping her, but have lacked everything since stopping.
options.note: Verses 17 to 18 record this exact claimed cause and effect, inverted from the truth Jeremiah states.

options.text: They claim the LORD personally commanded them to worship her.
options.note: They never claim the LORD commanded this worship; they credit the Queen of Heaven herself with their prosperity.

options.text: They claim it is required by Egyptian law.
options.note: No claim of Egyptian legal requirement is made; their reasoning is about remembered prosperity under her worship.

options.text: They claim Jeremiah himself once approved of the practice.
options.note: They never claim Jeremiah's approval; in fact they accuse him of speaking falsely against them.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah correct their claimed cause and effect?

options.text: He states that it was precisely their idolatry and disobedience to the LORD's voice that caused the disaster, not its interruption.
options.note: Verses 21 to 23 state this correction directly, naming disobedience as the actual cause.

options.text: He agrees that stopping the worship caused their troubles.
options.note: Jeremiah directly contradicts their claim, insisting idolatry itself, not its cessation, caused the disaster.

options.text: He says the disaster had no connection to their religious practices at all.
options.note: Jeremiah explicitly ties the disaster to their religious practice of idolatry, not to unrelated causes.

options.text: He refuses to answer and remains silent.
options.note: Jeremiah gives a direct, detailed answer in verses 20 to 23, not silence.

quiz.q: What sign does God give to prove whose word will stand, His or the people's?

options.text: The coming downfall of Pharaoh Hophra, delivered into the hands of his enemies just as Zedekiah was delivered to Nebuchadnezzar.
options.note: Verse 30 gives this specific, falsifiable sign naming Pharaoh Hophra by name.

options.text: An immediate famine that same week in Egypt.
options.note: The specific sign given is the future downfall of Pharaoh Hophra, not an immediate famine.

options.text: The rebuilding of Jerusalem's temple within the year.
options.note: No promise of imminent temple rebuilding appears in this passage; the sign concerns Pharaoh Hophra's downfall.

options.text: A message written on a scroll and buried at Tahpanhes.
options.note: The scroll and burial sign belongs to the previous chapter's stones symbolizing Nebuchadnezzar's throne, not this chapter's spoken sign about Pharaoh Hophra.

questions: The people credited a false goddess with prosperity that actually came from the LORD, and blamed disaster on the wrong cause entirely. Where might you be crediting the wrong source for blessings that are actually gifts from God?
This remnant rewrote their own history to justify continuing in sin. Where might you be quietly reshaping your memory of a hard season to avoid facing what actually needs to change in you?
The people said plainly, we will not listen to you, refusing correction even from God's own prophet. What correction from God's word are you currently resisting, and why?

God's patience with this generation had run its course after decades of warning and Jerusalem's own fall as an object lesson. How does this sober reality shape how seriously you take God's warnings in your own life right now?
Even in pronouncing severe judgment, God still promised a few fugitives would survive and return. Where do you need to trust that God's mercy remains real even in the middle of deserved consequences?

translationNotes.note: Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis, and Pathros name the main regions of Judean settlement in Egypt, from the northeastern delta down to Upper Egypt, showing the refugee community had already spread well beyond Tahpanhes alone by this point.

The Queen of Heaven is widely identified with Ishtar or Astarte, a Mesopotamian and Canaanite fertility and astral goddess whose worship, attested also in Jeremiah 7:18, apparently persisted as a household practice even among otherwise observant Judean families.

Pharaoh Hophra, known in Egyptian records as Apries, did in fact later face a military coup and was eventually killed by his own general Amasis, an outcome later writers connect to the fulfillment of this exact prophecy.
